families.s: HSE lifting-accessory selection, pre-use checking and thorough-examination guidance
families.t: chains, slings, hooks, eyebolts, SWL, angles, deterioration, competent examination, intervals, records and dangerous defects
f: Lifting accessories include chains, slings, ropes, hooks, shackles, eyebolts and similar load attachments.
Makeshift, badly worn, kinked, twisted, frayed or otherwise unsuitable accessories should not be used.
Safe working loads must not be exceeded and sling-leg forces increase as sling angle increases.
Pre-use checks should detect visible deterioration before an accessory is used.
Lifting accessories are normally thoroughly examined every six months unless an examination scheme specifies otherwise.
A thorough examination is a systematic detailed examination by a competent person followed by a written report.
Dangerous defects must be reported immediately and the item kept out of use until remedied.
Examination and inspection records should be protected and available to the dutyholder and enforcing authority.
families.g: Accessory risk depends on type and material, SWL, sling angle, load edges and temperature, wear and corrosion, identification, pre-use checks, examination and user competence.

families.s: HSE construction-hoist erection, use and examination guidance
families.t: goods versus passenger use, safe working load, erection, structural ties, gates, controls, operators, testing and inspection
f: Construction hoists include goods hoists, passenger hoists, inclined hoists and transport platforms.
Hoists should be sound, stable and capable of lifting the intended loads.
The permitted use, number of passengers and safe working load should be clearly marked.
Passengers must not ride on a goods-only hoist.
Erection should follow the manufacturer's instructions and be carried out by trained experienced people.
The hoist should be properly secured to its supporting structure.
Only trained competent people should operate the hoist.
Examination and testing are required after erection, significant alteration or repair and at relevant intervals.
families.g: Hoist risk depends on design, tower and ties, landing gates, controls, overload protection, load, erection, examination, maintenance, wind and operator competence.

families.s: HSE workplace passenger-lift, platform-lift and escalator guidance
families.t: LOLER scope, PUWER, workplace control, design conformity, maintenance, inspection, thorough examination, public users and escalators
f: Passenger and combined goods-passenger lifts used by workers are generally subject to LOLER.
Such lifts also require maintenance and inspection under applicable work-equipment duties.
Workplace passenger lifts require periodic thorough examination.
Equipment used mainly by the public may fall outside LOLER but businesses can still have safety responsibilities.
Escalators and moving walkways are not covered by LOLER but are covered by workplace welfare requirements.
New lifts, platform lifts and escalators must meet applicable supply and conformity requirements.
Lift owners should retain examination reports and act on defects affecting continued safe use.
Maintenance, landing protection, controls, rescue arrangements and user information should reflect the equipment and users.
families.g: Lift and escalator risk depends on equipment type, workplace or public use, doors and landing protection, controls, maintenance, examination, rescue, accessibility and user behaviour.

families.s: HSE machinery used to lift people and elevated-platform guidance
families.t: purpose-designed equipment, planning, carriers, fall and entrapment controls, exceptional use, supervision, maintenance and six-month examination
f: Lifting people creates higher risk and requires greater safety in design, use, maintenance and examination.
The correct purpose-designed equipment should be selected and the activity planned through risk assessment.
The carrier and equipment should prevent falls, crushing, entrapment, unintended release and overturning.
People operating or riding the equipment need suitable training and supervision.
Equipment not designed to lift people should be used for that purpose only in exceptional circumstances with additional precautions.
Lifting equipment used to lift people normally requires thorough examination every six months.
Pre-use checks and interim inspections may also be needed.
Emergency lowering, rescue, communication and exclusion arrangements should be established before lifting begins.
families.g: People-lifting risk depends on machine and carrier, purpose design, height and movement, fall and entrapment controls, stability, occupant capability, rescue, maintenance and examination.

families.s: HSE health and social-care moving-and-handling assessment guidance
families.t: worker and service-user injury, individual needs, task assessment, object handling, staffing, training, dignity, rehabilitation and review
f: Poor moving and handling can injure both workers and the person receiving care.
Risks include back pain, musculoskeletal disorders, handling accidents, discomfort and loss of dignity.
Employers must avoid hazardous manual handling where reasonably practicable and minimise remaining risk.
Assessments should consider the individual, task, environment, equipment and number of carers.
Care plans should record relevant handling needs and controls.
Workers need suitable training and supervision for the handling methods and equipment used.
An inflexible no-lifting policy can overlook individual needs and rehabilitation benefits.
Assessments should be reviewed when the person's condition, equipment, environment or care task changes.
families.g: Care-handling risk depends on person capability and behaviour, task, posture, environment, equipment, staffing, communication, worker competence and changing care needs.
